title: Poker Table Selection in Canada: Finding the Soft Games
excerpt: Table selection beats strategy for most online poker players. Here is how Canadians can find soft games, read the lobby stats and leave a table on time.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Most losing online poker players are not losing because their strategy is bad. They are losing because they sit down in the wrong games. Poker table selection is the least glamorous skill in the discipline and comfortably the most profitable one, because your win rate is determined less by how well you play than by how much worse than you the other people at the table are playing. For Canadian players choosing between regulated provincial rooms and international sites, learning to read a lobby properly is worth more than any amount of hand-chart memorisation.

Why table selection outperforms study

Poker is a zero-sum game before rake and negative-sum after it. Every dollar you win comes from another player at your table, which means your profit is a function of the mistakes available to be exploited, not of your absolute skill level. A competent regular in a game full of other competent regulars will grind out a tiny edge that rake will largely eat. The same player in a game with two recreational opponents will win at a multiple of that rate without changing a single decision.

This is uncomfortable for players who like to think of poker as a pure test of ability, but the arithmetic is not really disputable. Improving your play raises your ceiling. Improving your game selection raises your actual results, immediately, tonight.

The corollary nobody likes

If you are the weakest player at a table, someone else is doing exactly this to you. Honest self-assessment is part of the skill. A player who consistently seeks out the toughest available game because it feels like the serious thing to do is making the same error as a recreational player who sits anywhere — just in the opposite direction.

Reading the lobby before you sit

Every online poker lobby exposes a handful of statistics for each running table. They are the closest thing the game has to free information, and most players scroll straight past them.

  • Average pot size: the single most useful number. Large average pots relative to the blinds indicate loose, action-heavy play, which is where recreational money lives.
  • Players per flop: the percentage of hands where multiple players see a flop. High figures mean loose calling, which is the defining trait of a soft game. A table sitting well above the typical rate for its stake is worth a look.
  • Hands per hour: counter-intuitively, low hands-per-hour can be a good sign. Fast tables usually mean disciplined players folding quickly; slow tables mean people thinking, tanking and calling.
  • Waiting list length: a long queue often means other regulars have already identified the game. Sometimes that is a reason to join, sometimes a reason to look elsewhere.
  • Seats open: a table that has been running short-handed for a while, with nobody joining, usually means the regulars know something.

Sort the lobby by average pot size and players per flop rather than by stake, and you have done more for your win rate in ten seconds than an hour of theory video would deliver.

What a soft table actually looks like

Once you have sat down, the lobby statistics stop mattering and direct observation takes over. Play a few orbits without committing meaningful money and look for specific behaviours rather than a general vibe.

Recreational players tend to limp into pots rather than raising, call preflop raises from poor positions, take passive lines with strong hands, and make oversized or undersized bets that do not correspond to any consistent sizing scheme. They also frequently top up to odd stack sizes or play well below the full buy-in — a table with several short and irregular stacks is usually a table with several non-professionals.

Regulars are equally identifiable. They buy in for the maximum, sit in exactly 100 big blinds, three-bet from the blinds, and their bet sizings repeat. One or two at a table is normal. Four or five, and the game is not worth your time regardless of how well you think you play.

Position relative to the weak players

This is the detail that separates good table selection from adequate table selection. It is not enough that a soft player is at your table — you want them to your right, so that you act after them on every postflop street. If the two loose players are seated to your left and the two regulars are to your right, you have the worst possible arrangement and should consider changing seats or tables even though the game looks good in aggregate. Most rooms allow seat changes; use them.

The Canadian landscape in 2026

Where you play shapes what game selection is even possible. Ontario has run a licensed private-operator market since April 2022, and player pools there are ring-fenced to the province, which means smaller fields, fewer tables running at any given hour and a higher concentration of familiar names. That has real consequences: in a small pool, the regulars learn each other quickly, and the value of finding the recreational tables rises sharply because there are fewer of them. Our guide to 888poker in Ontario covers what the provincial pool means in practice for traffic and table availability.

Alberta joined the regulated market on July 13, 2026, adding a second province with licensed private operators. Elsewhere in the country, players are largely choosing between provincial lottery platforms and international rooms, each with different pool sizes and different regulatory recourse. Traffic patterns matter as much as the site itself — a room with a modest overall player count but a strong local following at your stake may offer better games than a larger one where you are a small fish in a professional pond.

Timing is table selection too

Games change character by the hour, and the pattern is consistent across sites. Weekday afternoons are the province of full-time players. Evenings, especially Friday and Saturday nights, bring recreational traffic. Large tournament series pull regulars away from cash tables, which quietly improves the cash games left behind. Major sporting events do the same in reverse, bringing casual crossover traffic into the poker client.

If your schedule allows any flexibility, playing during peak recreational hours rather than convenient professional hours is a structural edge that requires no skill at all. If it does not, at least know which kind of game you are walking into.

Leaving is a skill

Table selection does not end when you sit down. Games decay. The loose player who was funding the table busts and leaves, two regulars take the empty seats, and the game you carefully chose forty minutes ago no longer exists. Most players stay anyway, because leaving feels like quitting and because they want to win their money back from the specific opponents who took it.

Set a simple habit: every time a player leaves your table, reassess whether you would sit down in the game as it currently stands. If the answer is no, leave. There is nothing to recover at a specific table — your bankroll does not know or care which seat the money came from. Pair this with sensible bankroll discipline for your stake and you remove most of the ways that a good session turns into a bad one.

Multi-tabling and the selection trade-off

Adding tables raises your hourly volume but degrades your average table quality, because there are only so many good games running at once. A player grinding six tables is, by definition, sitting in several games they would not have chosen if they were playing one. For most players below the highest stakes, two to four carefully chosen tables produce a better hourly rate than six indiscriminate ones — and they leave enough attention free to actually notice when a game goes bad.

Putting it together

The routine is short. Sort the lobby by average pot size and players per flop. Join games with loose statistics and open seats to the left of the loose players. Observe for a few orbits before committing. Reassess whenever the table composition changes, and leave without ceremony when the game sours. Play during recreational hours where you can, and keep your table count low enough that selection remains meaningful. None of this is exciting. It is, reliably, where the money is.
